items.title: Quick ratio strips out the inventory you can't sell fast
items.claim: A retailer has current assets of £600,000 (including £400,000 inventory) and current liabilities of £300,000. What is the quick (acid-test) ratio?
items.reveal:
Quick ratio = (current assets - inventory) / current liabilities = (£600,000 - £400,000) / £300,000 = 0.67. Current ratio would be 2.0 — looking healthy. The acid-test reveals the firm could not cover short-term liabilities without selling stock.

The rule of thumb that quick ratio should exceed 1.0 is industry-dependent. Supermarkets routinely operate below 0.5 because they sell stock for cash before paying suppliers.
items.why: Two firms with identical current ratios can have very different real liquidity. Inventory turnover matters as much as the ratio number.

items.title: High gearing is risk, not failure
items.claim: A firm has long-term debt of £40 million and equity of £60 million. Its gearing ratio (debt / debt+equity) is 40%. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Gearing this high is always dangerous
Higher gearing magnifies returns to shareholders in good times and losses in bad — utilities routinely run 60%+ because cash flows are stable
Equity is always cheaper than debt

items.reveal:
UK water and electricity utilities (Severn Trent, National Grid) often carry gearing above 60% because regulated cash flows make debt servicing predictable. Tech firms (pre-2022) often had near-zero gearing because cash flows were volatile and equity was cheap.

Modigliani and Miller (1958) argued that, in perfect markets, capital structure is irrelevant. In real markets — with taxes, bankruptcy costs and asymmetric information — there is an optimal range. Lehman Brothers' gearing reached above 30:1 (debt:equity) before its 2008 collapse.
items.why: Whether high gearing is reckless depends on what cash flows look like. The number alone tells you little.

items.title: Share price and intrinsic value can diverge for years
items.claim: Robert Shiller's work (Nobel 2013) showed stock prices vary much more than fundamental dividends would justify. What's the implication for share price as a measure of company performance?

options.text: Share price always equals intrinsic value at all times
Share prices can diverge from intrinsic value for extended periods (excess volatility); managers focused on quarterly share prices may make worse long-term decisions
Share price has no link to fundamentals ever
Only private firms have intrinsic value

items.reveal_title: Markets price emotions as well as cash flows
items.reveal:
Shiller's 1981 American Economic Review paper showed S&P 500 prices fluctuated 5-13x more than dividend-based fair value would justify. Tech bubble peaks (2000, 2021) and crisis troughs (2009, 2020) bookend this excess volatility.

Warren Buffett quotes Benjamin Graham: 'In the short run the market is a voting machine, in the long run a weighing machine.' Managers paid largely in stock options can be incentivised to manage the voting machine rather than build long-term weight.
items.why: Headline share price moves often reflect investor sentiment as much as company performance. Compensation and strategy that anchor on share price import this volatility.
